messages.subject: Deterministic assignment of data to stochastic nodes?
messages.subject_clean: Deterministic assignment of data to stochastic nodes?
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to create a model with nodes for which values should be calculated deterministically from other nodes, but the probability of the nodes depends on a distribution. For a minimal example, imagine we are attempting to infer the intensity lambda of a Poisson process using data from a sampler with detection probability p. I've unsuccessfully tried:

library(nimble)

modelCode <- nimbleCode({

  for (i in 1:3) {
    y[i] ~ dpois(lambda = r)
    y_detected[i] <- y[i] * p
  }

  r ~ dgamma(10, 1)
  p ~ dbeta(10, 10)

})

set.seed(42)
n <- 3
samples <- round(rpois(n, lambda = 10) / 2)
data <- list(y_detected = samples)
constants <- list(n = n)
inits <- list(r = 7, p = 0.5)
m <- nimbleModel(modelCode,
                 constants = constants,
                 data = data,
                 inits = inits,
                 check = TRUE)

The above code results in the data I intended to supply for y_detected being overwritten with NA. I've also tried:
modelCode <- nimbleCode({

  for (i in 1:3) {
    y[i] ~ dpois(lambda = r)
    y[i] <- round(y_detected[i] / p)
  }

  r ~ dgamma(10, 1)
  p ~ dbeta(10, 10)

})

But the above results in multiple definitions of `y[i]`.

The complication is obviously that the value has to be updated as stochastic dependencies are sampled. What's the best way to code something like this?

Cheers,
Gregory

I may have figured this out. It seems that while

  for (i in 1:3) {
    y[i] ~ dpois(lambda = r)
    y_detected[i] <- y[i] * p
  }

inside the `nimbleCode` overwrites any data set as argument to `nimbleModel`, the solution is just to set the data after building the model with
m$setData(data)

I believe that the dependency graph is correct,

And running the model with a sufficiently large sample and iterations of the MCMC produces reasonable posterior distributions. There is something I'm still not understanding, though.
m$isDataVars
Returns a list with an element named for each variable: y, y_detected, p, and r. The values for y and y_detected reflect the number of nodes with those names. The values for p and r appear to be empty, however. They appear as `numeric(0)`. I don't understand the empty values, and I don't understand why m$isData("y") returns a vector of FALSE, while m$isData seems to suggest that it is being treated as data. Can someone please clarify? Or are there help files for these functions that I haven't found? Also, is it possible to inspect the likelihood function for a given node?

Cheers,
Gregory

messages.body_plain:
hi Gregory,

In NIMBLE, the notion of 'data' is for stochastic nodes for which one knows the values. I.e., for terms that contribute to the likelihood.

However, in your code:

    y[i] ~ dpois(lambda = r)
    y_detected[i] <- y[i] * p

'y_detected' here is deterministic and so it would not contribute to the likelihood.

On top of that, I would think that y_detected is integer-valued, but y[i]*p will be a real-valued number based on your code.

I don't know for sure what you intended / what makes sense for your context, but I would think that y_detected would be from a binomial distribution, like this:

   y[i] ~ dpois(lambda = r)

   y_detected[i] ~ dbin(p, y[i])

Then y[i] is latent and would be sampled as part of an MCMC, and you would set 'y_detected' to be data.

-Chris

messages.subject_clean: Two questions about nimble
messages.body_plain:
As far as setting up your model in NIMBLE, we don't provide ifelse() for use in model code. Instead, the best thing to do is write a
user-defined function that would fill in the values of T. This would have the great benefit of avoiding creating nodes in the model
graph for each element of T. Instead the function would fill in T and the entire T matrix would be treated as one node, which would
speed up various aspects of the computation. At the bottom of this email, I show an example of a user defined function for specifying
a covariance matrix in a Gaussian process setting. Hopefully it will be straightforward for you to modify that code for your case.

As far as a single function to run an MCMC, please see information on the nimbleMCMC function in our user manual or help(nimbleMCMC).
This allows you to take code for a model (or an existing model) and just run an MCMC without the intermediate steps, if you don't have
any interest in making modifications to the MCMC as is possible in the intermediate steps.

-chris

expcov <- nimbleFunction(
   run = function(dists = double(2), rho = double(0), sigma = double(0)) {
      returnType(double(2))
      n <- dim(dists)[1]
      result <- matrix(nrow = n, ncol = n, init = FALSE)
      sigma2 <- sigma*sigma
      for(i in 1:n)
            for(j in 1:n)
                  result[i, j] <- sigma2*exp(-dists[i,j]/rho)
      return(result)
})

code <- nimbleCode({
     mu0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
     sigma ~ dunif(0, 100)
     rho ~ dunif(0, 5)
     beta ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)

     mu[1:N] <- mu0*ones[1:N]
     cov[1:N, 1:N] <- expcov(dists[1:N, 1:N], rho, sigma)
     # dists is a (constant) matrix of pairwise distances between spatial locations
     s[1:N] ~ dmnorm(mu[1:N], cov = cov[1:N, 1:N])
     # likelihood
     for(i in 1:N) {
        lambda[i] <- exp(log(expected[i]) + beta*x[i] + s[i])
        y[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
    }
})
```

On Saturday, August 24, 2019 at 11:31:51 AM UTC-6, Vincent Landau wrote:
> Thanks very much Daniel! I'll give this a shot and post back to this thread if I have any issues.
>
> On Saturday, August 24, 2019 at 8:36:07 AM UTC-6, Daniel Turek wrote:
> > Vincent, thanks for your interest and use of NIMBLE.  I'm happy to hear about your plans for incorporating NIMBLE into your own R package(s).  I've done some work along the same lines, so let me try to provide some guidance for you.
> >
> > But first, one question.  In your initial post, you said you're trying to register a NIMBLE distribution from *within a package function*.  It might complicate things if your custom distribution(s) need to be defined *inside package function(s)*.  So, is it the case that (1) your custom distribution(s) are dynamic, that is, they depend on the argument(s) to package function(s)?  Or, (2) your distribution(s) are static, and fully known in advance, and thus could be defined inside your package, and subsequently be used inside your package function(s)?
> >
> > Assuming (2) is the case, which would be simpler, then, I would suggest the following:
> >
> > In your package NAMESPACE file, make sure (a) to import the nimble package, and (b) to export your custom distribution.  That is, include the lines:
> >
> > import(nimble)
> > export(dtvgeom)
> >
> > Heads up, you may also need to import the methods package:
> >
> > import(methods)
> >
> > In your package DESCRIPTION file, explicitly have your package "depend" on nimble.  That is, include the line, e.g.:
> >
> > Depends: R (>= 3.6.1),nimble
> >
> > Then, in your package R source files, (e.g., yourPackage / R / foo.R), include the definition of your custom distribution, making sure to export it.  So, that would look something like:
> >
> > #' Description of your distribution
> > #' ....
> > #' @export
> > dtvgeom <- nimbleFunction(
> >   run = function(...) {
> >     ...
> >   }, check = FALSE
> > )
> >
> > Including the "check = FALSE" will avoid warnings, in some cases.  It's safe to include that, if you're entirely confident the definition of your custom distribution is correct.
> >
> > Then, you'll be able to use the dtvgeom distribution inside your other package functions.
> >
> > Please let us know if anything here is unclear, and/or how it works for you.
> >
> > Cheers!  Keep in touch!
> > Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Thanks for your answer. I still have questions:

1. Below is the reproducible code,
Clearly the nimble's result is quite different from jag's results and original simulation.
Nimble's results (mean):
AR[1] AR[2] AR[3] AR[4] AR[5] AR[6] mu[1] mu[2] mu[3]
0.52148902 0.46670953 0.39335113 0.51637161 0.54331658 0.42711083 0.09051830 -0.13289888 -0.43612191
mu[4] mu[5] mu[6] rho sigma
0.06898406 0.17877351 -0.29512822 0.98052901 1.28362321

Jag's results(mean):
AR[1] AR[2] AR[3] AR[4] AR[5] AR[6] mu[1] mu[2] mu[3]
0.13896302 0.08892922 0.04474376 0.13590636 0.15708179 0.06119761 -1.11391869 -1.38906880 -1.75386173
mu[4] mu[5] mu[6] rho sigma
-1.13330403 -1.04101219 -1.59285866 0.64603896 0.22161486

Original settings (diferrent due to missing settings):
mu_b = c(-2,-2.5,-3,-2,-1.5,-3)
sd = rep(0.5,6)
cor[ii,jj]=0.5

It seems that nimble can't sample the posterior distribution thoroughly.
Do you know the reason?

library(rjags)
library(coda)
library(nimble)
library(mvtnorm)
###sim dataset
d = 6
nstudy = 20
pop_size <- 200
set.seed(123)
mu_b = c(-2,-2.5,-3,-2,-1.5,-3)
sd = rep(0.5,6)
sigma <- matrix(NA,nrow=d,ncol=d)
cor <- matrix(rep(1,d*d),nrow=d,ncol=d)
for(ii in 1:d){
  for(jj in 1:d){
    if(ii!=jj){cor[ii,jj]=0.5}
  }
}
for(ii in 1:d){
  for(jj in 1:d){
    sigma[ii,jj] <- cor[ii,jj]*sd[ii]*sd[jj]
  }
}
v <- rmvnorm(nstudy, rep(0, length = d), sigma)
rep.row<-function(x,n){
  matrix(rep(x,each=n),nrow=n)
}
mu <- rep.row(mu_b,nstudy)
pi1 <- exp(mu+v)/(1+exp(mu+v))
event <- matrix(NA,nrow=nstudy,ncol=d)
for(ii in 1:d){
  event[,ii] <- rbinom(nstudy,pop_size,pi1[,ii])
}
missing_pattern_determine <- function(event){
  d = 6
  nstudy = 20
    temp_event <- event[,1]
    temp_event <- cbind(temp_event,c(1:nstudy))
    colnames(temp_event) <- c("event","id")
    temp_event <- as.data.frame(temp_event)
    temp_event <- temp_event[with(temp_event, order(-event)), ]
    keep_study <- c(rep(3,4),rep(6,4),rep(2,4),rep(4,4),rep(5,4))
    non_missing_pattern <- matrix(0,nrow=nstudy,ncol=d)
    non_missing_pattern[,1]=1
    for(i in 1:nstudy){
      non_missing_pattern[temp_event[i,"id"],keep_study[i]] <- 1
    }
    return(non_missing_pattern)
}
set.seed(243)
non_missing_pattern <- missing_pattern_determine(event)
len <- sum(sum(non_missing_pattern))
s.id <http://s.id> <- rep(0,len)
t.id <http://t.id> <- rep(0,len)
event.n <- rep(0,len)
total.n <- rep(pop_size,len)
ind <- 1
for(i in 1:nstudy){
  for(j in 1:d){
    if(non_missing_pattern[i,j]!=0){
      s.id <http://s.id>[ind] <- i
      t.id <http://t.id>[ind] <- j
      event.n[ind] <- event[i,j]
      ind <- ind+1
    }
  }
}
ntrt <- d
r <- event.n
n <- total.n

##### jags results

## jags model
cat("model{

    for(i in 1:len){
    p[i]<-phi(vi[s[i],t[i]])
    r[i]~dbin(p[i],totaln[i])
    }
    for(j in 1:nstudy){
    vi[j,1:ntrt]~dmnorm(mu,T[1:ntrt,1:ntrt])
    }
    for(j in 1:ntrt){
    AR[j]<-phi(mu[j]/sqrt(1+pow(sigma,2)))
    mu[j]~dnorm(0,0.001)
    }
    sigma~dunif(0.0001,c)
    for(j in 1:ntrt){
    for(k in 1:ntrt){
    T[j,k]<-1/sigma^2*ifelse(j==k,diag,offdiag)
    }
    }

    diag<-(1+(ntrt-2)*rho)/(1+(ntrt-2)*rho-(ntrt-1)*rho^2)
    offdiag<-(-rho/(1+(ntrt-2)*rho-(ntrt-1)*rho^2))
    rho~dunif(-1/(ntrt-1),0.9999)

    }", file="jagsmodel.txt")

##
data.jags <- list(totaln = total.n, s = s.id <http://s.id>, t=t.id <http://t.id>, r=event.n, ntrt = ntrt, nstudy = nstudy, len=len, c=5)
Inits1=list(.RNG.name = "base::Mersenne-Twister", .RNG.seed = 123)
Inits2=list(.RNG.name = "base::Mersenne-Twister", .RNG.seed = 124)
Inits3=list(.RNG.name = "base::Mersenne-Twister", .RNG.seed = 125)
Inits4=list(.RNG.name = "base::Mersenne-Twister", .RNG.seed = 126)
inits.jags <- list(Inits1, Inits2, Inits3, Inits4)

start_time <- Sys.time()
jags <- jags.model(file="jagsmodel.txt",
                   data=data.jags,init=inits.jags,n.chains = 4,n.adapt = 5000)
update(jags, 10000)
codas1 <- coda.samples(jags,variable.names=c("AR", "mu", "sigma","rho"),
                       n.iter=20000,thin=10)
end_time <- Sys.time()
orig.time <- end_time - start_time

summary.stat <- summary(codas1)
gds <- gelman.diag(codas1,multivariate = FALSE)
effSS <- effectiveSize(codas1)
sum_fit1 <- cbind(cbind(summary.stat$statistics,summary.stat$quantiles),effSS,gds$psrf)
sum_fit1

##### nimble results
ecor_evar_cov <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(n = double(0), rho = double(0), sigma = double(0)) {
    returnType(double(2))

    result <- matrix(nrow = n, ncol = n, init = FALSE)
    sigma2 <- sigma*sigma
    for(i in 1:n){

      for(j in 1:n){
        if(i==j){
          result[i, j] <- sigma2}
        else{
          result[i, j] <- sigma2*rho}
      }
    }
    return(result)
  })
code.n <- nimbleCode(
  {
    rho ~ dunif(min=-1/(ntrt-1),max=0.9999)
    sigma ~ dunif(min=0.0001,max=c)

    for(j in 1:ntrt){
      mu[j]~dnorm(0,sqrt(1000))
    }

    cov[1:ntrt, 1:ntrt] <- ecor_evar_cov(ntrt, rho, sigma)

    for(i in 1:len){
      p[i]<-phi(vi[s[i],t[i]])
      r[i]~dbin(p[i],totaln[i])
    }

    for(j in 1:nstudy){

      vi[j,1:ntrt]~dmnorm(mu[1:ntrt],cov=cov[1:ntrt, 1:ntrt])

    }

    for(j in 1:ntrt){
      AR[j]<-phi(mu[j]/sqrt(1+pow(sigma,2)))
    }

  }

)

constants.n <- list(ntrt = ntrt, nstudy = nstudy, len=len, c=5)
data.n <- list(totaln = total.n, s = s.id <http://s.id>, t=t.id <http://t.id>, r=event.n)
inits.n <- list(rho=runif(1,0,0.99),sigma =runif(1,0.0001,5),mu=rnorm(ntrt,0,5))

Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code.n, constants.n, data.n, inits.n)

Rmodel$calculate()

conf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel)
conf$printSamplers()

## add your monitors
conf$addMonitors(c("mu","AR","sigma","rho"))

Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(conf)

Cmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Rmodel)

seed.n <- c(1,5,10,20)
start_time <- Sys.time()
samples <- runMCMC(Cmcmc, setSeed=seed.n,
                   thin = 10,niter = 35000, nburnin = 15000, nchains = 4,
                   samplesAsCodaMCMC=TRUE)
end_time <- Sys.time()
nimble.time <- end_time - start_time

summary.stat <- summary(samples)
gds <- gelman.diag(samples,multivariate = FALSE)
effSS <- effectiveSize(samples)
sum_fit3 <- cbind(cbind(summary.stat$statistics,summary.stat$quantiles),effSS,gds$psrf)
sum_fit3

2. second question is about compiling the model.
In stan, once we compile the model, if we change the data and constants, we don't need to compile the model again.
How can we do that in nimble:

Cmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Rmodel)
samples <- runMCMC(Cmcmc, setSeed=seed.n,
                   thin = 10,niter = 35000, nburnin = 15000, nchains = 4,
                   samplesAsCodaMCMC=TRUE)

> As far as setting up your model in NIMBLE, we don't provide ifelse() for use in model code. Instead, the best thing to do is write a
> user-defined function that would fill in the values of T. This would have the great benefit of avoiding creating nodes in the model
> graph for each element of T. Instead the function would fill in T and the entire T matrix would be treated as one node, which would
> speed up various aspects of the computation. At the bottom of this email, I show an example of a user defined function for specifying
> a covariance matrix in a Gaussian process setting. Hopefully it will be straightforward for you to modify that code for your case.
>
> As far as a single function to run an MCMC, please see information on the nimbleMCMC function in our user manual or help(nimbleMCMC).
> This allows you to take code for a model (or an existing model) and just run an MCMC without the intermediate steps, if you don't have
> any interest in making modifications to the MCMC as is possible in the intermediate steps.
>
> -chris
>
>

>    run = function(dists = double(2), rho = double(0), sigma = double(0)) {

>         lambda[i] <- exp(log(expected[i]) + beta*x[i] + s[i])

messages.body_plain:
Vincent, I'm happy to hear you're still working on this.

The very short answer to your question is: yes, you should call registerDistributions(...) to register your custom distribution for use with NIMBLE, inside whatever package function(s) will make use of this distribution, prior to any call to nimbleModel() to create a nimble model object which uses your distribution.  Let me know if that's not clear.

Cheers,
Daniel

> Hi all,
>
> Thanks for your helpful guidance so far. I'm finally picking this back up after a period of intense work on some other projects. Exporting the distribution to the namespace is straightforward enough, but do I still need to run registerDistributions somewhere in the package function? It's really important that the function be compiled to C++ to improve speed.
>

> Vincent

> On Saturday, August 24, 2019 at 11:31:51 AM UTC-6, Vincent Landau wrote:
> > Thanks very much Daniel! I'll give this a shot and post back to this thread if I have any issues.
> >
> > On Saturday, August 24, 2019 at 8:36:07 AM UTC-6, Daniel Turek wrote:
> > > Vincent, thanks for your interest and use of NIMBLE.  I'm happy to hear about your plans for incorporating NIMBLE into your own R package(s).  I've done some work along the same lines, so let me try to provide some guidance for you.
> > >
> > > But first, one question.  In your initial post, you said you're trying to register a NIMBLE distribution from *within a package function*.  It might complicate things if your custom distribution(s) need to be defined *inside package function(s)*.  So, is it the case that (1) your custom distribution(s) are dynamic, that is, they depend on the argument(s) to package function(s)?  Or, (2) your distribution(s) are static, and fully known in advance, and thus could be defined inside your package, and subsequently be used inside your package function(s)?
> > >
> > > Assuming (2) is the case, which would be simpler, then, I would suggest the following:
> > >
> > > In your package NAMESPACE file, make sure (a) to import the nimble package, and (b) to export your custom distribution.  That is, include the lines:
> > >
> > > import(nimble)
> > > export(dtvgeom)
> > >
> > > Heads up, you may also need to import the methods package:
> > >
> > > import(methods)
> > >
> > > In your package DESCRIPTION file, explicitly have your package "depend" on nimble.  That is, include the line, e.g.:
> > >
> > > Depends: R (>= 3.6.1),nimble
> > >
> > > Then, in your package R source files, (e.g., yourPackage / R / foo.R), include the definition of your custom distribution, making sure to export it.  So, that would look something like:
> > >
> > > #' Description of your distribution
> > > #' ....
> > > #' @export
> > > dtvgeom <- nimbleFunction(
> > >   run = function(...) {
> > >     ...
> > >   }, check = FALSE
> > > )
> > >
> > > Including the "check = FALSE" will avoid warnings, in some cases.  It's safe to include that, if you're entirely confident the definition of your custom distribution is correct.
> > >
> > > Then, you'll be able to use the dtvgeom distribution inside your other package functions.
> > >
> > > Please let us know if anything here is unclear, and/or how it works for you.
> > >
> > > Cheers!  Keep in touch!
> > > Daniel
> > >
> > >
> > >

messages.subject: Re: Two questions about nimble
messages.subject_clean: Two questions about nimble
messages.body_plain:
Hi Simon,

In your nimble code you define the covariance using the nimbleFunction. In your jags code you define the precision (T).
It's not clear to me that those two definitions specify the same model (i.e., is the covariance you construct equal
to the inverse of T?

I would think the easiest thing to do is set up the nimbleFunction so that it constructs the T matrix equivalently
to what you have in your model code for the jags implementation.

As far as not recompiling, you can always access and modify model variables in the compiled model like a typical R object.
If cModel is a compiled model, you can say

cModel$my_data <- some_new_values
cModel$my_covariate <- some_other_new_values

etc.  Then you can run whatever algorithm you want on the model with the revised values.

-chris

docker run -it --rm \
    -v "$(pwd)":/home/tvgeomMCMC \
    -e USER=tvgeomMCMC \
    -e PASSWORD=tvgeomMCMC \
    -p 8664:8787 \

Then open up http://localhost:8664 in a browser and enter tvgeomMCMC for user and password when prompted (this may all be info you already know but just wanted to be thorough).

You should be able to replicate the issue by running the following code in a fresh R session:

devtools::install()
library(tvgeomMCMC)
data <- simulate_tvgeom(n = 100,
                        t = 50,
                        covariates = NA,
                        intercept = -4,
                        beta = c(0.1, 0.8, -2.2),
                        censored = TRUE)

draws <- tvgeom_mcmc(y = data$y,
                     covariates = data$covariates,
                     beta_start = c(-5, 0, 0, 0),
                     n_iter = 100,
                     n_burnin = 10)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Vincent--

Could you do something as simple as

if (k == 1) {
  Beta[indices] ~ dnorm(...)
} else {

  for (i in 1:k) {

    Beta[indices[i]] ~ dnorm(...)
  }
}

If k and indices are both provided as a constant my understanding is that the if statement can be handled when the model is built. I had success with the following.

toycode <-
  nimbleCode({
  if (k == 1) {
    Beta[indices] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
  } else {

    for (i in 1:k)

    Beta[indices[i]] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
  }
})

mod <- nimbleModel(code = toycode,
                   constants = list(k = 3,
                                    indices = c(1,2,4)),
                   data = list(Beta = c(1,2,0.5,0.4,0,-1,2,-3,-2,1,0, 0,0)))
mod$calculate()
Cmod <- compileNimble(mod)
Cmod$calculate()

mod <- nimbleModel(code = toycode,
                   constants = list(k = 1,
                                    indices = c(1)),
                   data = list(Beta = c(1,2,0.5,0.4,0,-1,2,-3,-2,1,0, 0,0)))
mod$calculate()
Cmod <- compileNimble(mod)
Cmod$calculate()

Ben

messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to get the posterior distributions of some parameters from a model run, and I'm running into memory issues. Specifically, `as.matrix(mcmcC$mvSamples)` fails with the message "Error: vector memory exhausted (limit reached?)". I can try giving R more memory as suggested in this StackOverflow answer <https://stackoverflow.com/questions/51295402/r-on-macos-error-vector-memory-exhausted-limit-reached>,  and then re-running the model, but I'd like a more general solution if there is one. Can I extract chains for subsets of nodes and save them to disk somehow?

Cheers,
Gregory

Will it make sense to increase the thinning interval (thin)?

If, as is common, you have a small number of nodes for which you want a large sample and a large number of nodes, such as latent states, for which you can get by with a smaller sample, you can use the monitors2 (second set of monitored variables), which can have a separate (larger) thinning interval (thin2).

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
One additional comment, if setting a thin interval, and potentially use of both {montiors, thin}, and {monitors2, thin2} still don't full solve your problem: MCMC "monitors" are at the variable level, so you only have the option to monitor complete variables (e.g., a full vector, or a full array).  However, if you're only interested in posterior samples for a small number of elements of a large vector, or a large array, then you could certainly "re-express" the model, such that the components you're interested in posterior samples for are (alone, themselves) contained in a different, smaller, variable.  Then, you would only monitor that variable, the smaller one of interest, and potentially reduce the memory requirements a lot.

I'm guessing there is some further context here, like nested loops, that prevents you from simply not using the for loop.

You could try using a definition-time if-then-else, like

if( length(indices) > 1) {
  for(i in 1:indices) {
     x[i] ~ ...
  }
} else {
    x[1] ~ ...
}

The condition (length(indices) > 1) will be evaluated during nimbleModel, in the R environment (so indices will not be taken from constants).  The result will be as if only one of the outcomes was written in the model code.

hi Simon,

I looked at some output from jags and nimble when using
`non_missing_pattern <- missing_pattern_determine(event)`, and the
MCMC
output looks similar to me between jags and nimble. So I'm not sure
what you're seeing when you say they give different results.

Side note (but potentially helpful for improving  computational
efficiency): it is best to set 's' and 't' in 'constants' rather than
in 'data'.
Otherwise nimble thinks that the dependency structure can change
because 's' and 't' could change, which can result in additional
unneeded calculations. You can also set 'totaln' in constants.

As far as the second question, if you are changing constants (in
particular the number of items in a for loop or the size of any
variables)
then you would need to recreate the model and recompile. If you are
only changing values of data or covariates (specified via 'inits' or
'data', not 'constants')
then you could do as I suggested. You might be able to arrange things
so that you group simulations that have the same sizes and only
recompile when you need to change sizes.

Cmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Rmodel)

Cmodel$varName <- some_value
Cmcmc$run(1000)

Cmodel$varName <- some_other_value
## you may want to think at this point about what initial values you
want for the MCMC and possibly reset the relevant parameter values
Cmcmc$run(1000)

-chris

>>>>
>>>> As far as setting up your model in NIMBLE, we don't provide ifelse() for use in model code. Instead, the best thing to do is write a
>>>> user-defined function that would fill in the values of T. This would have the great benefit of avoiding creating nodes in the model
>>>> graph for each element of T. Instead the function would fill in T and the entire T matrix would be treated as one node, which would
>>>> speed up various aspects of the computation. At the bottom of this email, I show an example of a user defined function for specifying
>>>> a covariance matrix in a Gaussian process setting. Hopefully it will be straightforward for you to modify that code for your case.
>>>>
>>>> As far as a single function to run an MCMC, please see information on the nimbleMCMC function in our user manual or help(nimbleMCMC).
>>>> This allows you to take code for a model (or an existing model) and just run an MCMC without the intermediate steps, if you don't have
>>>> any interest in making modifications to the MCMC as is possible in the intermediate steps.
>>>>
>>>> -chris
>>>>
>>>>
>>>> expcov <- nimbleFunction(
>>>>    run = function(dists = double(2), rho = double(0), sigma = double(0)) {
>>>>       returnType(double(2))
>>>>       n <- dim(dists)[1]
>>>>       result <- matrix(nrow = n, ncol = n, init = FALSE)
>>>>       sigma2 <- sigma*sigma
>>>>       for(i in 1:n)
>>>>             for(j in 1:n)
>>>>                   result[i, j] <- sigma2*exp(-dists[i,j]/rho)
>>>>       return(result)
>>>> })
>>>>
>>>> code <- nimbleCode({
>>>>      mu0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
>>>>      sigma ~ dunif(0, 100)
>>>>      rho ~ dunif(0, 5)
>>>>      beta ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
>>>>
>>>>      mu[1:N] <- mu0*ones[1:N]
>>>>      cov[1:N, 1:N] <- expcov(dists[1:N, 1:N], rho, sigma)
>>>>      # dists is a (constant) matrix of pairwise distances between spatial locations
>>>>      s[1:N] ~ dmnorm(mu[1:N], cov = cov[1:N, 1:N])
>>>>      # likelihood

>>>>         lambda[i] <- exp(log(expected[i]) + beta*x[i] + s[i])

I have a custom distribution that I register with nimble, so I have a script inside of the R/ folder that just has all of those nimbleFunctions defined. Something about them being nimble functions causes covr to ignore those lines of code (if no R functions are in the script, it ignores the script entirely). This results in those lines not being considered in coverage reports (e.g. generated for covr.io <http://covr.io>).
> > > >
> > > > I'm guessing it's much more complicated that it might seem at first glance, but I wanted to flag it here just so devs and others are aware. I did find a hacky workaround that I'll use in the meantime. See the following basic example.

> > > > r_function_add <- function(a, b) {
> > > >   return(a + b)
> > > > }
> > > > nimble_function_add <- nimbleFunction(
> > > >   run = function(a = double(1), b = double(1)) {
> > > >     returnType(double(0))
> > > >     return(r_function_add(a, b))
> > > >   }
> > > > )
> > > >
> > > > Then, testthat tests can be run on nimble_function_add() and coverage corresponding to R_function_add() will be reported.

messages.subject: Spatial Capture Recapture with partial identities
messages.subject_clean: Spatial Capture Recapture with partial identities
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to see if I can fit various spatial partial identity models in NIMBLE that are currently only implemented in my R-based samplers. Most of these models are extensions of unmarked SCR, so I think the first step is to see if I can fit unmarked SCR in NIMBLE. A caveat is that I need to probabilistically reconstruct the capture history instead of marginalizing over the individuals.

Unmarked SCR is typical SCR where the individual identities are lost. The data are typically summarized by n, the trap by occasion counts, or just the trap-level counts. To include observation-level partial identity covariates, I will need to work with the latent identity samples one by one. The true individual by trap capture history is latent:

y.true[i,j]~Poisson(K*lamd[i,j]) where lamd[i,j] is the individual by trap expected count, a function of the distance between activity center i and trap j. We observe matrix y.obs of dimension n.obs x J where n.obs is the total number of latent identity counts, sum(y.true). Each row corresponds to an observation with a single 1 indicating the trap of capture. Another way to represent this would be to have y.obs be a vector of length n.obs listing the trap of capture for each observation.

We can create a map from y.obs to y.true, call it ID. ID is a vector of length n.obs indicating the individual identity that each sample is currently assigned to. We can construct y.true from y.obs ID by:

 y.true=matrix(0,nrow=M,ncol=J)
 for(i in 1:length(ID)){
   y.true[ID[i],]=y.true[ID[i],]+y.obs[i,]
 }

In R, I update y.true by iterating through the rows of y.obs, or a subset of these rows, on each iteration and switching their individual identities. This is a Gibbs update:

 up=sample(1:n.samples,nswap,replace=FALSE) #which latent data observations will we update? Could just update all of them.
        for(l in up){
          nj=which(y.obs[l,]>0) #which trap is the sample recorded in?
          possible=which(z==1)#Can only swap the sample with z=1 individuals
          #there will be more constraints here limiting possible swaps when I introduce the partial identity covariates

          #construct full conditional
          njprobs=lamd[,nj]
          njprobs[setdiff(1:M,possible)]=0
          njprobs=njprobs/sum(njprobs) #this is the full conditional

          newID=sample(1:M,1,prob=njprobs) #sample new identity for this observation

          #update y.true if we didn't propose the same ID it already has
          if(ID[l]!=newID){
            swapped=c(ID[l],newID)
            #update y.true
            y.true[ID[l],]=y.true[ID[l],]-y.obs[l,] #subtract this observation from current ID
            y.true[newID,]=y.true[newID,]+y.obs[l,] #add this observation to new ID
            ID[l]=newID
            ll.y[swapped,]= dpois(y.true[swapped,],K*lamd[swapped,],log=TRUE) #update observation model likelihood
          }
        }

Can this or something similar be done in NIMBLE? I appreciate any help and will be happy to provided more information, if needed.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: nimbleOptions and nimbleInternalFunctions not found for package built on nimble
messages.body_plain:
hi Vincent,

The brief answer here is to put 'nimble' into 'Depends', not 'Imports'
in DESCRIPTION.

When your code calls nimbleModel(), we are creating a bunch of
functions for each node in the model that allow calculation of the
density of that node, simulation from that node, etc. These functions
are created in a reference class for the model that we dynamically
generate. What that means is that the reference class is not part of
the nimble namespace (because it was created in the context of your
package) but those functions that we generate do use functions from
the nimble namespace.  So nimble itself needs to be loaded in order
for the functions from the nimble namespace to be found.

I'll bring this up with our development team for us to think a bit
more about whether it would make sense to rearrange things so nimble
can be in 'Imports'.

chris

Just adding that this

> Including the "check = FALSE" will avoid warnings, in some cases.  It's safe to include that, if you're entirely confident the definition of your custom distribution is correct.

ended up being critical for getting the package to pass the check() stage. Without it, devtools::document() resulted in the following:
Warning messages:
1: For this nimbleFunction to compile, these objects must be defined as nimbleFunctions, nimbleFunctionLists, or nimbleLists before compilation: dtvgeom_nimble.
2: For this nimbleFunction to compile, these objects must be defined as nimbleFunctions, nimbleFunctionLists, or nimbleLists before compilation: ptvgeom_nimble.
3: For this nimbleFunction to compile, these objects must be defined as nimbleFunctions, nimbleFunctionLists, or nimbleLists before compilation: qtvgeom_nimble.

which was causing devtools::check() to fail.

I just wanted to document that here in case anyone runs into a similar problem in the future.

Thanks so much to everyone for all the help throughout this process!

- Vincent

Very helpful indeed, Vincent.  In the past I included the "check = FALSE" only to suppress the extra output, but I wasn't aware it facilitates passing devtools:check().  Thanks for sharing this for the benefit of everyone.

As always, please keep in touch with any successes and/or challenges you run into while using NIMBLE.

Daniel

>
> > Including the "check = FALSE" will avoid warnings, in some cases.  It's safe to include that, if you're entirely confident the definition of your custom distribution is correct.

messages.subject: Re: Spatial Capture Recapture with partial identities
messages.subject_clean: Spatial Capture Recapture with partial identities
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

Yes it should be possible.  Let me sketch how you would do it.  You will need to fill in a meaningful model to have a working example, so I haven't tested this.

I'll assume in the model you have something like
for(i in 1:N)
    ID[i] ~ dcat(prior_probs[1:N])
where prior_probs could be set in the constants list in nimbleModel, or it could be a variable in the model.

And I assume you are using the ID elements as stochastic indices, say like this (but I know your SCR model is different)
  for(i in 1:N) {
    y[i] ~ dnorm( mu[ ID[i] ], sd = 1)

You can translate your sampler to a nimble sampler that is compilable and compatible with the MCMC system like this:

ID_sampler <- nimbleFunction(
  name = "ID_sampler",
  contains = sampler_BASE,
  setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control) { ## Required arguments. setup is run once when the MCMC is built.
    N <- length(model$y)
    probs <- rep(1/N, N) ## for drawing random integers
    ## target should be "ID".
    ##  The names are hard-coded below but could be generalized, but anyway target is used two lines down.
    nSwap <- control$nSwap ## how many trials to do each time the sampler is run
    calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(target) ## This could be broken down to individual ones, but as a simple demonstration, I'm using all together
  },
  run = function() {
    ## for uncompiled execution, you can put a browser() in here and check what is happening
    for(i in 1:nSwap) {
      l <- rcat(1, probs) ## We don't support compilation of sample(), so I'm using rcat instead.
      nj <- which(model$y.obs[l,]>0) ## This will be a length-1 vector
      possible <- which(model$z == 1)
     ## setdiff is not supported for compilation, so I re-arranged how to get the result you need, IIUC
      njProbs <- numeric(0, length = N)
      njProbs[ possible ] <- model$lamb[possible, nj]
      newID <- rcat(1, njProbs)
      if(model$ID[l] != newID) {
        model$y.true[model$ID[l],] <<- model$y.true[model$ID[l],]- model$y.obs[l,] #subtract this observation from current ID
        model$y.true[model$newID,] <<- model$y.true[newID,]+model$y.obs[l,] #add this observation to new ID
        model$ID[l]=newID
      }
    }
    model$calculate(calcNodes) ## This updates the log probabilities in the model
    nimCopy(model, mvSaved, nodes = calcNodes, row = 1, logProb = TRUE) ## This updates the saved states of the model
  }
)

Once you have used "model <- nimbleModel(...)", you would do as follows

MCMCconf <- configureMCMC(model)
MCMCconf$printSamplers() ## inspect default samplers
MCMCconf$removeSamplers("ID") ## remove default samplers for ID
MCMCconf$addSampler(type = ID_sampler, target = "ID", control = list(nSwap = 10)) ## add your new sampler
MCMCconf$printSamplers() ## inspect modified samplers
MCMC <- buildMCMC(MCMCconf) ## build the MCMC from the configuration
MCMCrun(niter = 10) ## debug by running it uncompiled

## When you are happy with it, you can skip uncompiled testing and compile and run
Cmodel <- compileNimble(model)
CMCMC <- compileNimble(MCMC, project = model) ## the compiled MCMC will use the compiled model
CMCMC$run(niter)

I don't immediately see why a Gibbs update with no model probability calculations makes sense, but that's for you to be clear on.

If you get it working, if nSwap is small, it could be more efficient to calculate and copy only the swapped nodes and their dependencies, but I've used all nodes for now.

HTH

-Perry

On Wed, Nov 13, 2019 at 12:38 PM Ben Augustine <baug...@vt.edu> wrote:

> I am trying to see if I can fit various spatial partial identity models in NIMBLE that are currently only implemented in my R-based samplers. Most of these models are extensions of unmarked SCR, so I think the first step is to see if I can fit unmarked SCR in NIMBLE. A caveat is that I need to probabilistically reconstruct the capture history instead of marginalizing over the individuals.
>
> Unmarked SCR is typical SCR where the individual identities are lost. The data are typically summarized by n, the trap by occasion counts, or just the trap-level counts. To include observation-level partial identity covariates, I will need to work with the latent identity samples one by one. The true individual by trap capture history is latent:
>
> y.true[i,j]~Poisson(K*lamd[i,j]) where lamd[i,j] is the individual by trap expected count, a function of the distance between activity center i and trap j. We observe matrix y.obs of dimension n.obs x J where n.obs is the total number of latent identity counts, sum(y.true). Each row corresponds to an observation with a single 1 indicating the trap of capture. Another way to represent this would be to have y.obs be a vector of length n.obs listing the trap of capture for each observation.
>
> We can create a map from y.obs to y.true, call it ID. ID is a vector of length n.obs indicating the individual identity that each sample is currently assigned to. We can construct y.true from y.obs ID by:
>
>  y.true=matrix(0,nrow=M,ncol=J)
>  for(i in 1:length(ID)){
>    y.true[ID[i],]=y.true[ID[i],]+y.obs[i,]
>  }
>
> In R, I update y.true by iterating through the rows of y.obs, or a subset of these rows, on each iteration and switching their individual identities. This is a Gibbs update:
>
>
>  up=sample(1:n.samples,nswap,replace=FALSE) #which latent data observations will we update? Could just update all of them.
>         for(l in up){
>           nj=which(y.obs[l,]>0) #which trap is the sample recorded in?
>           possible=which(z==1)#Can only swap the sample with z=1 individuals
>           #there will be more constraints here limiting possible swaps when I introduce the partial identity covariates
>
>           #construct full conditional
>           njprobs=lamd[,nj]
>           njprobs[setdiff(1:M,possible)]=0
>           njprobs=njprobs/sum(njprobs) #this is the full conditional
>
>           newID=sample(1:M,1,prob=njprobs) #sample new identity for this observation
>
>           #update y.true if we didn't propose the same ID it already has
>           if(ID[l]!=newID){
>             swapped=c(ID[l],newID)
>             #update y.true
>             y.true[ID[l],]=y.true[ID[l],]-y.obs[l,] #subtract this observation from current ID
>             y.true[newID,]=y.true[newID,]+y.obs[l,] #add this observation to new ID
>             ID[l]=newID
>             ll.y[swapped,]= dpois(y.true[swapped,],K*lamd[swapped,],log=TRUE) #update observation model likelihood
>           }
>         }
>
> Can this or something similar be done in NIMBLE? I appreciate any help and will be happy to provided more information, if needed.
>
> Ben
>

The User Manual / vignette linked from the compareMCMCs github page shows how to include a new summary statistic (a "metric").  IIRC, thinning is done before the metric is calculated.  Choice of summaries/metrics is not currently splittable by nodes.

e.g.
timeModelCode <- nimbleCode({
  x[1] ~ dnorm(mu_0, 1)
  y[1] ~ dnorm(x[1], 1)

messages.body_plain:
Got it.  Back to your original questions then: no, the "samples" and "summary" are intimately connected.  You cannot get "summary statistics" for nodes which are not monitored (have samples recorded) by the MCMC.  So if you want summary statistics for your (large number of) deterministic nodes, you'll have to monitor those deterministic nodes.

The set of "summary statistics" is really just a post-processing step performed on the recorded samples.  The statistics could be modified if need be; but I think the bigger answer is that you'd have to ask the MCMC to monitor all your deterministic nodes, in order to calculate summary statistics for them, regardless of whether you ask the MCMC to return the samples to you.

Last: summary statistics are calculated using the post-thinning samples (since those are the only ones recorded by the MCMC, hence they are the ones used to calculate summary statistics).

Does that answer your questions?

It is just a derived parameter describing how the observed data are currently allocated to individuals. There is nothing I can say about it in the main Nimble model.

3) Is it possible to do multiple MH updates in a loop inside one call to a custom update? I am currently doing multiple Gibbs updates, but they don't require the likelihood to be updated before the next ID update. See below in green.

Main model code.

####NIMBLE model
NimModel <- nimbleCode({

  lam0~dunif(0,10)
  sigma~dunif(0,10)
  psi~dunif(0,1)

  for(i in 1:M) {
    z[i] ~ dbern(psi)
    s[i,1] ~ dunif(xlim[1],xlim[2])

    lam[i,1:J] <- GetDetectionRate(s = s[i,1:2], X = X[1:J,1:2], J=J,

                                   sigma=sigma, lam0=lam0, z=z[i],ID=ID[1:n.samp])

    for(j in 1:J) {
      y[i,j] ~ dpois(K*lam[i,j])

  # for(l in 1:n.samp){

  # }

})#model

Custom capture history update:

## sampler to jointly update y[1:M,j,k] so that they sum to n[j,k]
IDSampler <- nimbleFunction(

 contains = sampler_BASE,
 setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control) {
   # Defined stuff

   y.obs<-control$y.obs

   j<-control$j
   M<-control$M
   calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(target)
 },

 run = function() {
   lam.curr <- model$lam[1:M,j] #individual by trap expected counts

   fullcond <- lam.curr[1:M]/sum(lam.curr[1:M])

   idx=which(y.obs==j) #which samples are at this trap?
   if(length(idx)>0){
     for(i in 1:length(idx)){ #update them one by one
       ID.curr <- model$ID[idx[i]]
       ID.prop <- rcat(1,fullcond[1:M])
       #subtract out old ID obs
       model$y[ID.curr,j] <<- model$y[ID.curr,j]-1
       #add in new ID obs
       model$y[ID.prop,j] <<- model$y[ID.prop,j]+1
       #swap in new ID
       model$ID[idx[i]] <<- ID.prop
     }
     # calculate logProb after Gibbs updates

     model_lp_proposed <- model$calculate(calcNodes)
     copy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)
   }
 },
 methods = list( reset = function () {} )
)

I may not follow everything but here goes.

On Tue, Nov 19, 2019 at 3:56 PM Ben Augustine <baug...@vt.edu> wrote:
> I'm now updating the latent capture history one observation at a time (necessary to add partial identity covariates later) and have 3 questions.
>
> 1) Is there a way to not call the custom capture history update for traps with no samples? Currently, I'm aborting inside of the custom update. Color coded red below. Can I just remove the sampler to update the capture histories for those traps and not supply a new one?
>

It looks right now (following my initial reply, where I was adapting your R code) that you have a single sampler responsible for all the custom updates.  In that case, doing some kind of check to avoid unnecessary effort, as you do, or passing in a vector of indices needing sampling effort, is the solution I see.

Another way you could go, building from the basic idea you now have working, would be to modify the custom sampler to do just one index and have a separate copy of the sampler for each index that needs sampling.  That is similar to what happens with our standard samplers; there is one sampler object for each node to be sampled.  To create that, you would use "addSampler" for indices that need sampling (and not others), i.e. for traps with samples.  A convenient way to get node names for adding (or removing, using removeSampler), is model$expandNodeNames("lam"), for example.

> 2) I don't know how to correctly supply "ID" as data with an init when ID is not referenced in the main NIMBLE model, but only in a custom MCMC update. I am able to get it to work by  saying ID is required in a custom function where I don't in fact use it (color coded blue below). ID is used and updated in the custom capture history update. It is just a derived parameter describing how the observed data are currently allocated to individuals. There is nothing I can say about it in the main Nimble model.

One way to think of the model is as a data structure that caches calculations.  I think you are saying you need ID to be in the data structure, but you don't need it to do anything meaningful in the model graph.  In that case, just get it declared somewhere.  Putting it artificially on the right-hand side of a declaration as you've done will do the trick.  An alternative would be to uncomment the lines with the uniform prior.  That will get it into the model and the uniform prior, even if ever calculated, will not influence anything.

>
> 3) Is it possible to do multiple MH updates in a loop inside one call to a custom update? I am currently doing multiple Gibbs updates, but they don't require the likelihood to be updated before the next ID update. See below in green.

You can do anything valid that you want.  The rules (documented in the manual) are that, upon entry, you can expect that both the model and mvSaved are in the same state, which is up to date.  Upon exit, your sampler must leave both the model and mvSaved in the same state, again up to date.  If you implement multiple MH updates internal to one "sampler", that is fine as long as you know what you are doing.  It is (not recommended but) possible to violate the rules if you know your samplers will come in sequence in the sampler list (you can see the sampler order by MCMCconf$printSamplers();  you can access sampling assignment internals by MCMCconf$getSamplers();  you can modify the order of samplers by MCMCconf$setSamplers();  you can also modify this order before running the MCMC, but this gets into more internals so I'll stop for now).  In that case, as long as the last of your samplers leaves model and mvSaved in sync upon exit, before any other samplers you didn't write are called, you're good.  That is definitely *not* recommended, but I'm just saying it to highlight how the system works.

The User Manual is long but should have a lot of these details.

>
> Main model code.
>
> ####NIMBLE model
> NimModel <- nimbleCode({
>
>   lam0~dunif(0,10)
>   sigma~dunif(0,10)
>   psi~dunif(0,1)
>
>   for(i in 1:M) {
>     z[i] ~ dbern(psi)
>     s[i,1] ~ dunif(xlim[1],xlim[2])
>     s[i,2] ~ dunif(ylim[1],ylim[2])
>     lam[i,1:J] <- GetDetectionRate(s = s[i,1:2], X = X[1:J,1:2], J=J,
>                                    sigma=sigma, lam0=lam0, z=z[i],ID=ID[1:n.samp])
>     for(j in 1:J) {
>       y[i,j] ~ dpois(K*lam[i,j])
>     }#j
>    }#i
>   ncap <- Getncap(y=y[1:M,1:J],z=z[1:M],M=M,J=J)
>   N <- sum(z[1:M])
>   # for(l in 1:n.samp){
>   #   ID[l]~dunif(0,M)
>   # }
>
>
> })#model
>
>
> Custom capture history update:
>
> ## sampler to jointly update y[1:M,j,k] so that they sum to n[j,k]
> IDSampler <- nimbleFunction(
>  contains = sampler_BASE,
>  setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control) {
>    # Defined stuff
>    y.obs<-control$y.obs
>    j<-control$j
>    M<-control$M
>    calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(target)
>  },
>
>  run = function() {
>    lam.curr <- model$lam[1:M,j] #individual by trap expected counts
>    fullcond <- lam.curr[1:M]/sum(lam.curr[1:M])
>    idx=which(y.obs==j) #which samples are at this trap?
>    if(length(idx)>0){
>      for(i in 1:length(idx)){ #update them one by one
>        ID.curr <- model$ID[idx[i]]
>        ID.prop <- rcat(1,fullcond[1:M])
>        #subtract out old ID obs
>        model$y[ID.curr,j] <<- model$y[ID.curr,j]-1
>        #add in new ID obs
>        model$y[ID.prop,j] <<- model$y[ID.prop,j]+1
>        #swap in new ID
>        model$ID[idx[i]] <<- ID.prop
>      }
>      # calculate logProb after Gibbs updates
>      model_lp_proposed <- model$calculate(calcNodes)
>      copy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)
>    }
>  },
>  methods = list( reset = function () {} )
> )
>
> On Wednesday, November 13, 2019 at 3:38:54 PM UTC-5, Ben Augustine wrote:
> > I am trying to see if I can fit various spatial partial identity models in NIMBLE that are currently only implemented in my R-based samplers. Most of these models are extensions of unmarked SCR, so I think the first step is to see if I can fit unmarked SCR in NIMBLE. A caveat is that I need to probabilistically reconstruct the capture history instead of marginalizing over the individuals.
> >
> > Unmarked SCR is typical SCR where the individual identities are lost. The data are typically summarized by n, the trap by occasion counts, or just the trap-level counts. To include observation-level partial identity covariates, I will need to work with the latent identity samples one by one. The true individual by trap capture history is latent:
> >
> > y.true[i,j]~Poisson(K*lamd[i,j]) where lamd[i,j] is the individual by trap expected count, a function of the distance between activity center i and trap j. We observe matrix y.obs of dimension n.obs x J where n.obs is the total number of latent identity counts, sum(y.true). Each row corresponds to an observation with a single 1 indicating the trap of capture. Another way to represent this would be to have y.obs be a vector of length n.obs listing the trap of capture for each observation.
> >
> > We can create a map from y.obs to y.true, call it ID. ID is a vector of length n.obs indicating the individual identity that each sample is currently assigned to. We can construct y.true from y.obs ID by:
> >
> >  y.true=matrix(0,nrow=M,ncol=J)
> >  for(i in 1:length(ID)){
> >    y.true[ID[i],]=y.true[ID[i],]+y.obs[i,]
> >  }
> >
> > In R, I update y.true by iterating through the rows of y.obs, or a subset of these rows, on each iteration and switching their individual identities. This is a Gibbs update:
> >
> >
> >  up=sample(1:n.samples,nswap,replace=FALSE) #which latent data observations will we update? Could just update all of them.
> >         for(l in up){
> >           nj=which(y.obs[l,]>0) #which trap is the sample recorded in?
> >           possible=which(z==1)#Can only swap the sample with z=1 individuals
> >           #there will be more constraints here limiting possible swaps when I introduce the partial identity covariates
> >
> >           #construct full conditional
> >           njprobs=lamd[,nj]
> >           njprobs[setdiff(1:M,possible)]=0
> >           njprobs=njprobs/sum(njprobs) #this is the full conditional
> >
> >           newID=sample(1:M,1,prob=njprobs) #sample new identity for this observation
> >
> >           #update y.true if we didn't propose the same ID it already has
> >           if(ID[l]!=newID){
> >             swapped=c(ID[l],newID)
> >             #update y.true
> >             y.true[ID[l],]=y.true[ID[l],]-y.obs[l,] #subtract this observation from current ID
> >             y.true[newID,]=y.true[newID,]+y.obs[l,] #add this observation to new ID
> >             ID[l]=newID
> >             ll.y[swapped,]= dpois(y.true[swapped,],K*lamd[swapped,],log=TRUE) #update observation model likelihood
> >           }
> >         }
> >
> > Can this or something similar be done in NIMBLE? I appreciate any help and will be happy to provided more information, if needed.
> >
> > Ben
>

Hi Daniel,

Yes, that answered my questions and it made sense. Thanks. It does lead me to another question along the same line, though. Perhaps this falls under the category of "feature request".

Would it be possible to implement monitors that do not retain any samples? I am thinking specifically of the Boost Accumulators library that I mentioned in my previous message. The accumulators retain only the information needed to calculate whatever quantities are needed. For example, I'd like to estimate the mean and variance of those nodes using something like Welford's online algorithm <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_calculating_variance>. It seems like this would not break the concept of a monitor as something that is triggered when a node is updated, and then does something, like store the new value in a data structure or use the new value to perform some calculation and then discard it, or anything else.

Cheers,
Gregory

Fantastic.  I like the idea a lot, and will consider it as a future addition to the MCMC.  The short answer, is that (within reason) anything is possible, and it's just a matter of implementing it.  A feature like this (perhaps called "accumulators" ?) could be made available through the lowest-level invocation of the MCMC, specifically, using mcmc$run().

Without having looked at the reference you sent, just one quick question - would the only "accumulators" we'd be interested in, perhaps, be "running total sum", and "running total sum of squares"?  I ask, because (1) I think those would be sufficient for calculating mean and variance, as you suggest, and (2) from an implementation standpoint, it would be a lot simpler if the only types of "accumulators" allowed were restricted to those two (fixed, predefined, and finite-in-number) types.  It would be a lot more (implementation) effort to allow for fully general "accumulators", e.g., "sum of log-logs", or whatever otherwise.

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I'm implementing this method from Mike Meredith's website into a SCR model and I'm running into a strange issue. Similar to Glenn, I receive
Warning: dynamic index out of bounds: habMat[trunc(S[i, 1]), trunc(S[i, 2])].

My code is slightly different and looks more like this:
    S[i,1] ~ dunif(1, upperLimit[1]) # priors for the activity centers for each individual
    S[i,2] ~ dunif(1, upperLimit[2]) # lower x and y coordinates = 1
    pOK[i] <- habMat[trunc(S[i,1]), trunc(S[i,2])]

    OK[i] ~ dbern(pOK[i])     # OK[i] = 1, the ones trick

To reduce calculation time, I tweak the values of upperLimit prior to assigning them to constants by subtracting 0.00001. Where upperLimit is a numeric vector with 2 values pertaining to the dimensions of the habitat mask with 1 added. For example, my habitat mask is a matrix with dimensions c(59,42) so the upperLimit values = c(59.99999, 42.99999).
  In most of the model runs thus far, this has worked great. The most recent run has caused the above warning message to appear. When I look at the values created by the MCMC run, many of them are VERY far outside the min/max values, ie some values areas much/little as -1208451.77.

My question is: Why is the Uniform distribution allowing values to be estimated outside the prescribed min/max provided in S[i,1] ~ dunif(1, upperLimit[1])?

I see in the previous post that Perry gave a fix, but this creates extra nodes that the model has to calculate, which I want to avoid given that I'm already running into memory issues when compiling the model and long MCMC estimation times. Is there an alternative that would not create extra nodes in the model?

Many thanks,
Colby

On Thursday, August 23, 2018 at 11:11:35 AM UTC-6, Glenn Stauffer wrote:
> Ah, I found the mistake, and it is obvious in the warning itself! Apparently I did change the code after all. The offending line:
>
>  pOK[i] <- m[trunc(S[i, 1] + 1), trunc(S[i, 2] + 1)]
>
> should be:
>
>  pOK[i] <- m[trunc(SX[i]+1),trunc(SY[i]+1)]
>
> And then it works.

In that case, doing some kind of check to avoid unnecessary effort, as you do, or passing in a vector of indices needing sampling effort, is the solution I see.
>
> Another way you could go, building from the basic idea you now have working, would be to modify the custom sampler to do just one index and have a separate copy of the sampler for each index that needs sampling.  That is similar to what happens with our standard samplers; there is one sampler object for each node to be sampled.  To create that, you would use "addSampler" for indices that need sampling (and not others), i.e. for traps with samples.  A convenient way to get node names for adding (or removing, using removeSampler), is model$expandNodeNames("lam"), for example.

It is just a derived parameter describing how the observed data are currently allocated to individuals. There is nothing I can say about it in the main Nimble model.
>
> One way to think of the model is as a data structure that caches calculations.  I think you are saying you need ID to be in the data structure, but you don't need it to do anything meaningful in the model graph.  In that case, just get it declared somewhere.  Putting it artificially on the right-hand side of a declaration as you've done will do the trick.  An alternative would be to uncomment the lines with the uniform prior.  That will get it into the model and the uniform prior, even if ever calculated, will not influence anything.

If you implement multiple MH updates internal to one "sampler", that is fine as long as you know what you are doing. That is definitely *not* recommended, but I'm just saying it to highlight how the system works.

> >     }#j
> >    }#i
> >   ncap <- Getncap(y=y[1:M,1:J],z=z[1:M],M=M,J=J)

> >  setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control) {
> >    # Defined stuff
> >    y.obs<-control$y.obs
> >    j<-control$j
> >    M<-control$M
> >    calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(target)
> >  },
> >
> >  run = function() {
> >    lam.curr <- model$lam[1:M,j] #individual by trap expected counts
> >    fullcond <- lam.curr[1:M]/sum(lam.curr[1:M])
> >    idx=which(y.obs==j) #which samples are at this trap?
> >    if(length(idx)>0){
> >      for(i in 1:length(idx)){ #update them one by one
> >        ID.curr <- model$ID[idx[i]]

> >        model$y[ID.curr,j] <<- model$y[ID.curr,j]-1
> >        #add in new ID obs

> >        #swap in new ID

> >      }

Most of these models are extensions of unmarked SCR, so I think the first step is to see if I can fit unmarked SCR in NIMBLE. A caveat is that I need to probabilistically reconstruct the capture history instead of marginalizing over the individuals.
> > >
> > > Unmarked SCR is typical SCR where the individual identities are lost. The data are typically summarized by n, the trap by occasion counts, or just the trap-level counts. To include observation-level partial identity covariates, I will need to work with the latent identity samples one by one. The true individual by trap capture history is latent:
> > >
> > > y.true[i,j]~Poisson(K*lamd[i,j]) where lamd[i,j] is the individual by trap expected count, a function of the distance between activity center i and trap j. > > >
> > >

messages.subject: Re: Error: dynamic index out of bounds
messages.subject_clean: Error: dynamic index out of bounds
messages.body_plain:
Hi Colby,

This is somewhat hard to diagnose, partly because it's not a fully reproducible example, and I guess that's because you've described it as an idiosyncratic phenomenon.  The best I can do is give some tips and suggestions.

If it only occurs in some runs, then you could experiment with set.seed(<pick a number>) to find a random number seed that reproduces the problem.  That would give us something to work with.

If the message is generated during nimbleModel(), then it is occurring during uncompiled (i.e. pure R) execution of the model's calculations (and if you don't need that, use calculate=FALSE for a faster model build). That means all R debugging tools are available.  For example you could debug MCMC$run and step through the samplers to look at S[i, 1:2] values as they are updated.  But before diving into that level, you could start by inspecting the model.  Specifically, look at model$S and see if any values are outside of the bounds.  That would indicate some problem with initial values.

In general, nimble tends to be hungrier for valid initial values than is JAGS.  That has to do (at least partly) with default sampler choices.  Are you providing inits for S, and are they definitely valid?

It is also possible that if some other part of the model does not have valid inits, then the initial total log probability (likelihood, if you prefer) is -Inf, in which case some samplers may behave crazily.  You can check with model$getLogProb().  You can check specific parts of the model such as model$getLogProb('S')  (or model$calculate(S), if you've changed any values).

What I suspect is happening with the pathological values in the chain is that once an S[i, 1:2] value gets outside of the valid range, then a sampler will flail and move it around meaninglessly.  If it starts in the valid range, then a move outside the valid range should never be accepted.  That's why I suspect a problem with initial values.

Summary: Setting up a reproducible example is key.  Invalid inits are always worth considering as a cause of basic model problems.

-Perry

messages.subject: Re: Questions about configuring MCMC for returned samples and summary stats
messages.subject_clean: Questions about configuring MCMC for returned samples and summary stats
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gregory,

As an immediate option if you want to accomplish your goal, if you are game to modify a nimbleFunction, you can do the following:

Go to nimble source code, R/MCMC_build.R (https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/blob/master/packages/nimble/R/MCMC_build.R).  This is the nimbleFunction for an MCMC.  It manages calling the list of samplers and collecting outputs.

Make a local copy of this nimbleFunction and insert what you want in the master loop, starting at line 188.  The nimCopy lines are where samples for monitors are saved in the mvSamples (output).

If you want an accumulator to be available afterward, create it first in the setup code.  Example:

In setup code:
myAccumulator <- 0

In run code, in the master loop, do whatever accumulation step(s) you need, like:
myAccumulator <- myAccumulator + model$x[1] ## or whatever

Then, after you build the MCMC, you will be able to access myAccumulator as
MCMC$myAccumulator
in either the compiled or uncompiled version.

You can add getter and setter methods for myAccumulator if it helps.

If you need myAccumulator to be a vector, it is important to create it in setup code with length > 1 so the compiler knows for sure it is a vector:
myAccumulator <- c(0, 0)

Then use your local version of buildMCMC instead of the package version.

HTH
Perry

Great.  While you're "thinking about [the set of accumulators] and coming back", let me add another question for you:

In your mind, would the specific values accumulated (getting added together) be tied to the thinning interval?  That is, if thin=10, we only "add up" every 10th sample -- even if we're not *recording* (monitoring) the samples?  This would be more natural in terms of implementation, and also more obvious regarding the question "how many samples were accumulated?, that is, how many did we add together?", since it's the same number as the number of rows in the samples array.

That said, since accumulators wouldn't actually be tied intimately to the monitors (that's the idea, right), it perhaps would make more sense to add together *all* samples, regardless of thinning (this begs a further question: what about pre-burn-in samples?).  In the case of accumulating every sample, regardless of whatever thinning is taking place for the monitored samples, I'd perhaps also maintain another variable, simply giving the "number of samples that were accumulated, in the cumulative sum", so that the answer to the question "how many samples were accumulated" is obvious and transparent.

Your thoughts, Gregory, are welcomed.

messages.body_plain:
hi Gregory,

The main thing is that if you want to parallelize across MCMC chains or some other algorithm applied to a given model, you need to create separate copies of the model (via nimbleModel()), compiled model, and uncompiled and compiled algorithm (e.g., the MCMC). I.e., do not do "model2 <- model1", as nimble models and algorithms are copied by reference, so model2 would just point to the same model values as model1. (We're working on enhancements that will allow for easier parallelization, but for now, that's how things are.)

As far as nodes/cpus/tasks, I would just think of each MCMC chain as a separate SLURM task. As far as memory, it's really a matter of how much a given model+algorithm needs.

And, no we don't provide support for GPUs.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
If you're using the PF as part of particle MCMC then NIMBLE will just sample the missing observations as part of the MCMC. So I think that should work fine.

If you're just applying a PF directly, not as part of an MCMC, that won't work as some likelihood terms would be NA. You might instead be able to set up the model
so there are no nodes for the missing observations, and I suspect that would work, but haven't thought carefully about it. Happy to discuss further if this is of interest.

-chris

> On Sunday, 17 November 2019 17:56:43 UTC, Tom Hull wrote:
> > Hi
> >
> > Pretty sure I'm missing something obvious, but how do I extract the samples for the latent states when using the `RW_PF_block` MCMC sampler?
> >
> > e.g.
> > timeModelCode <- nimbleCode({
> >   x[1] ~ dnorm(mu_0, 1)
> >   y[1] ~ dnorm(x[1], 1)
> >   for(i in 2:t){
> >     x[i] ~ dnorm(x[i-1] + c, pro_error)
> >     y[i] ~ dnorm(x[i], obs_error)
> >   }
> >
> >   pro_error ~ dnorm(0, 1)
> >   obs_error ~ dnorm(0, 1)
> >   c ~ dnorm(1,1)
> >   mu_0 ~ dnorm(0, 1)
> > })
> >
> > # simulate some data
> > seed = 159
> > t <- 25
> > mu_0 <- -10
> > pro_error <- 0.01
> > obs_error <- 0.5
> > x <- rnorm(1 ,mu_0, pro_error)
> > y <- rnorm(1, x, obs_error)
> > c <- 1;
> > for(i in 2:t){
> >   x[i] <- rnorm(1, x[i-1] + c, pro_error)
> >   y[i] <- rnorm(1, x[i], obs_error)
> > }
> >
> > # build the model
> > rTimeModel <- nimbleModel(timeModelCode, constants = list(t = t),
> >                           data <- list(y = y), check = FALSE )
> >
> > cTimeModel <- compileNimble(rTimeModel)
> >
> > timeConf <- configureMCMC(rTimeModel)
> >
> > # Add random walk PMCMC sampler with particle number optimization.
> > timeConf$addSampler(target = c("obs_error", "pro_error", "c", "mu_0"), type = "RW_PF_block",
> >                     control <- list(propCov= diag(4), adaptScaleOnly = FALSE,
> >                                     pfType = "auxiliary", pfControl = list(saveAll = T, smoothing = T),

> > CtimeConf <- compileNimble(RtimeConf, project=rTimeModel, resetFunctions=T)
> > CtimeConf$run(500)
> >
> > CtimeConf$mvSamples # This doesn't contain "x"!
> >
> > Many Thanks
> >

messages.subject: Re: Spatial Capture Recapture with partial identities
messages.subject_clean: Spatial Capture Recapture with partial identities
messages.body_plain:
OK, I've made a lot of progress and I'm almost done transferring one progressively complex set of spatial partial identity models to NIMBLE, unmarked SCR -> categorical SPIM -> categorical SPIM with observation error in category levels -> genotype SPIM.

One (hopefully) last thing I'm unsure about is how to handle a specific set of parameters that I house in a list in my R-based sampler. I transferred another set of parameters from a list structure to a ragged matrix for use in NIMBLE, which works, but if I want to record the posteriors, it also records the matrix indices that are not used, which isn't ideal. The set of parameters is a list of matrices that could be of length over 100 for specific applications. The NIMBLE documentation seems to suggest that the only way to access list elements is to subset by name, e.g., pi$locus1, pi$locus2, etc. This will be very tedious if there are 100 or so list elements.

So my question is, is there a workaround where I can index lists by their numeric index?

Thanks.

Ben

On Thursday, November 21, 2019 at 10:42:31 AM UTC-5, Ben Augustine wrote:

> Much appreciated, Perry! I think I know enough now to stop bugging you!
>
> Ben
>

> On Tue, Nov 19, 2019 at 7:23 PM Perry de Valpine <pdeva...@berkeley.edu> wrote:

> > I may not follow everything but here goes.
> >

> > On Tue, Nov 19, 2019 at 3:56 PM Ben Augustine <baug...@vt.edu> wrote:
> > > I'm now updating the latent capture history one observation at a time (necessary to add partial identity covariates later) and have 3 questions.
> > >
> > > 1) Is there a way to not call the custom capture history update for traps with no samples? Currently, I'm aborting inside of the custom update. Color coded red below. Can I just remove the sampler to update the capture histories for those traps and not supply a new one?
> > >
> >
> > It looks right now (following my initial reply, where I was adapting your R code) that you have a single sampler responsible for all the custom updates.  In that case, doing some kind of check to avoid unnecessary effort, as you do, or passing in a vector of indices needing sampling effort, is the solution I see.
> >
> > Another way you could go, building from the basic idea you now have working, would be to modify the custom sampler to do just one index and have a separate copy of the sampler for each index that needs sampling.  That is similar to what happens with our standard samplers; there is one sampler object for each node to be sampled.  To create that, you would use "addSampler" for indices that need sampling (and not others), i.e. for traps with samples.  A convenient way to get node names for adding (or removing, using removeSampler), is model$expandNodeNames("lam"), for example.
> >
> > > 2) I don't know how to correctly supply "ID" as data with an init when ID is not referenced in the main NIMBLE model, but only in a custom MCMC update. I am able to get it to work by  saying ID is required in a custom function where I don't in fact use it (color coded blue below). ID is used and updated in the custom capture history update. It is just a derived parameter describing how the observed data are currently allocated to individuals. There is nothing I can say about it in the main Nimble model.
> >
> > One way to think of the model is as a data structure that caches calculations.  I think you are saying you need ID to be in the data structure, but you don't need it to do anything meaningful in the model graph.  In that case, just get it declared somewhere.  Putting it artificially on the right-hand side of a declaration as you've done will do the trick.  An alternative would be to uncomment the lines with the uniform prior.  That will get it into the model and the uniform prior, even if ever calculated, will not influence anything.
> >
> > >
> > > 3) Is it possible to do multiple MH updates in a loop inside one call to a custom update? I am currently doing multiple Gibbs updates, but they don't require the likelihood to be updated before the next ID update. See below in green.
> >
> > You can do anything valid that you want.  The rules (documented in the manual) are that, upon entry, you can expect that both the model and mvSaved are in the same state, which is up to date.  Upon exit, your sampler must leave both the model and mvSaved in the same state, again up to date.  If you implement multiple MH updates internal to one "sampler", that is fine as long as you know what you are doing.  It is (not recommended but) possible to violate the rules if you know your samplers will come in sequence in the sampler list (you can see the sampler order by MCMCconf$printSamplers();  you can access sampling assignment internals by MCMCconf$getSamplers();  you can modify the order of samplers by MCMCconf$setSamplers();  you can also modify this order before running the MCMC, but this gets into more internals so I'll stop for now).  In that case, as long as the last of your samplers leaves model and mvSaved in sync upon exit, before any other samplers you didn't write are called, you're good.  That is definitely *not* recommended, but I'm just saying it to highlight how the system works.
> >
> > The User Manual is long but should have a lot of these details.
> >

> > >
> > > Main model code.
> > >
> > > ####NIMBLE model
> > > NimModel <- nimbleCode({
> > >
> > >   lam0~dunif(0,10)
> > >   sigma~dunif(0,10)
> > >   psi~dunif(0,1)
> > >
> > >   for(i in 1:M) {
> > >     z[i] ~ dbern(psi)
> > >     s[i,1] ~ dunif(xlim[1],xlim[2])
> > >     s[i,2] ~ dunif(ylim[1],ylim[2])
> > >     lam[i,1:J] <- GetDetectionRate(s = s[i,1:2], X = X[1:J,1:2], J=J,
> > >                                    sigma=sigma, lam0=lam0, z=z[i],ID=ID[1:n.samp])
> > >     for(j in 1:J) {
> > >       y[i,j] ~ dpois(K*lam[i,j])
> > >     }#j
> > >    }#i
> > >   ncap <- Getncap(y=y[1:M,1:J],z=z[1:M],M=M,J=J)
> > >   N <- sum(z[1:M])
> > >   # for(l in 1:n.samp){
> > >   #   ID[l]~dunif(0,M)
> > >   # }
> > >
> > >
> > > })#model
> > >
> > >
> > > Custom capture history update:
> > >
> > > ## sampler to jointly update y[1:M,j,k] so that they sum to n[j,k]
> > > IDSampler <- nimbleFunction(
> > >  contains = sampler_BASE,
> > >  setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control) {
> > >    # Defined stuff
> > >    y.obs<-control$y.obs
> > >    j<-control$j
> > >    M<-control$M
> > >    calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(target)
> > >  },
> > >
> > >  run = function() {
> > >    lam.curr <- model$lam[1:M,j] #individual by trap expected counts
> > >    fullcond <- lam.curr[1:M]/sum(lam.curr[1:M])
> > >    idx=which(y.obs==j) #which samples are at this trap?
> > >    if(length(idx)>0){
> > >      for(i in 1:length(idx)){ #update them one by one
> > >        ID.curr <- model$ID[idx[i]]
> > >        ID.prop <- rcat(1,fullcond[1:M])
> > >        #subtract out old ID obs
> > >        model$y[ID.curr,j] <<- model$y[ID.curr,j]-1
> > >        #add in new ID obs
> > >        model$y[ID.prop,j] <<- model$y[ID.prop,j]+1
> > >        #swap in new ID
> > >        model$ID[idx[i]] <<- ID.prop
> > >      }
> > >      # calculate logProb after Gibbs updates
> > >      model_lp_proposed <- model$calculate(calcNodes)
> > >      copy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)
> > >    }
> > >  },
> > >  methods = list( reset = function () {} )
> > > )
> > >
> > > On Wednesday, November 13, 2019 at 3:38:54 PM UTC-5, Ben Augustine wrote:
> > > > I am trying to see if I can fit various spatial partial identity models in NIMBLE that are currently only implemented in my R-based samplers. Most of these models are extensions of unmarked SCR, so I think the first step is to see if I can fit unmarked SCR in NIMBLE. A caveat is that I need to probabilistically reconstruct the capture history instead of marginalizing over the individuals.
> > > >
> > > > Unmarked SCR is typical SCR where the individual identities are lost. The data are typically summarized by n, the trap by occasion counts, or just the trap-level counts. To include observation-level partial identity covariates, I will need to work with the latent identity samples one by one. The true individual by trap capture history is latent:
> > > >
> > > > y.true[i,j]~Poisson(K*lamd[i,j]) where lamd[i,j] is the individual by trap expected count, a function of the distance between activity center i and trap j. We observe matrix y.obs of dimension n.obs x J where n.obs is the total number of latent identity counts, sum(y.true). Each row corresponds to an observation with a single 1 indicating the trap of capture. Another way to represent this would be to have y.obs be a vector of length n.obs listing the trap of capture for each observation.
> > > >
> > > > We can create a map from y.obs to y.true, call it ID. ID is a vector of length n.obs indicating the individual identity that each sample is currently assigned to. We can construct y.true from y.obs ID by:
> > > >
> > > >  y.true=matrix(0,nrow=M,ncol=J)
> > > >  for(i in 1:length(ID)){
> > > >    y.true[ID[i],]=y.true[ID[i],]+y.obs[i,]
> > > >  }
> > > >
> > > > In R, I update y.true by iterating through the rows of y.obs, or a subset of these rows, on each iteration and switching their individual identities. This is a Gibbs update:
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >  up=sample(1:n.samples,nswap,replace=FALSE) #which latent data observations will we update? Could just update all of them.
> > > >         for(l in up){
> > > >           nj=which(y.obs[l,]>0) #which trap is the sample recorded in?
> > > >           possible=which(z==1)#Can only swap the sample with z=1 individuals
> > > >           #there will be more constraints here limiting possible swaps when I introduce the partial identity covariates
> > > >
> > > >           #construct full conditional
> > > >           njprobs=lamd[,nj]
> > > >           njprobs[setdiff(1:M,possible)]=0
> > > >           njprobs=njprobs/sum(njprobs) #this is the full conditional
> > > >
> > > >           newID=sample(1:M,1,prob=njprobs) #sample new identity for this observation
> > > >
> > > >           #update y.true if we didn't propose the same ID it already has
> > > >           if(ID[l]!=newID){
> > > >             swapped=c(ID[l],newID)
> > > >             #update y.true
> > > >             y.true[ID[l],]=y.true[ID[l],]-y.obs[l,] #subtract this observation from current ID
> > > >             y.true[newID,]=y.true[newID,]+y.obs[l,] #add this observation to new ID
> > > >             ID[l]=newID
> > > >             ll.y[swapped,]= dpois(y.true[swapped,],K*lamd[swapped,],log=TRUE) #update observation model likelihood
> > > >           }
> > > >         }
> > > >
> > > > Can this or something similar be done in NIMBLE? I appreciate any help and will be happy to provided more information, if needed.
> > > >
> > > > Ben
> > >
